summary.title: Qwen-AgentWorld: Language World Models for General Agents

details: LLM-agent research has focused almost entirely on the policy (state→action), leaving no general-purpose world model for language/agentic environments (state, action → next state).
Real environments cannot offer turn-level scalability or controllability (targeted perturbations, infeasible/irreversible domains).

Qwen-AgentWorld (35B-A3B and 397B-A17B): a 'native' language world model that, given a unified textual trajectory schema (system prompt with task/action space/initial state/demonstrations/simulation instruction plus interaction history and current action), predicts the next environment observation via long chain-of-thought, unifying seven agentic domains (MCP, Search, Terminal, SWE, Android, Web, OS) in one model with GUI states as accessibility trees / view hierarchies.

Trained end-to-end for environment simulation under the principle 'CPT injects, SFT activates, RL sharpens' — continual pre-training on state-transition trajectories plus professional world-knowledge corpora, SFT to activate next-state-prediction reasoning, and RL with hybrid rubric-and-rule rewards.
AgentWorldBench: a companion benchmark of real-environment ground-truth observations for reference-grounded rubric judging of language world models.

10M+ environment interaction trajectories from dedicated agent infrastructure (sandboxes, MCP servers, persistent terminal/Android/browser/desktop VMs), cleaned open interaction traces, and in-house agentic trajectories; disjoint pools per stage.

CPT adds specialized world-knowledge corpora (law, medicine, finance, cybersecurity, industrial control, current affairs) and uses turn-level information-theoretic loss masking: four token-overlap statistics (overlap, novelty, Jaccard, length ratio) assign turns to 7 categories with keep ratios from 5% (echo) to 100% (retrieval).

SFT: 7,094 thinking trajectories from 10,250 candidates (69.2% retention) via best-of-3 rejection sampling with judge scoring, 256k context, prompt-template diversification across 10 variants; system-prompt templates generated by an automated 'AutoResearch' propose–evaluate–refine loop (12 runs x 10 iterations, v0–v11 assigned disjointly to RL/CPT/SFT).

RL: GSPO, 92,308 samples (avg 19.4k prompt tokens, 13.4 turns), prompts capped at 128k; reward = 9:1 mix of a five-dimensional LLM-judge rubric (each 1–5) and executable rule-based binary verifiers; one prediction turn per trajectory.

2,170 samples across 7 domains, built from agentic trajectories of 5 frontier agents (mainly Claude Opus 4.6; Claude Sonnet 4.5 for an early subset; 3 Qwen models for GUI) on 9 established benchmarks (e.g., Tool Decathlon, Terminal-Bench 1.0 & 2.0, OSWorld-Verified, in-house SWE), with ground-truth observations from real execution; data-source-level train/test partitioning.

Turn sampling: first + last + 3 intermediate turns per trajectory, then 50% random subsample; text domains 72.4% of samples, each GUI domain 9.2%; contexts from 12.9k (Terminal) to 59.3k tokens (MCP).

Scoring: reference-grounded LLM judge on Format, Factuality, Consistency, Realism, Quality (mean scaled to 0–100), with domain-specific rubrics and three-way content classification (deterministic / pre-existing / runtime metadata) to avoid false negatives; GPT-5.2 selected as judge via double-blind Turing-test accuracy.

14 baselines: frontier proprietary (Claude Opus 4.8/4.6, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro), open-weight (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.6, GLM-5.1, MiniMax-M2.7), and Qwen-family checkpoints without LWM training (Qwen3.5/3.6 variants) that isolate the training effect.
Temperature 0.6, thinking mode on, max context/generation at each model's limit; open-weight models served with SGLang.

concrete_detailed_setting.aspect: Application I: world model as decoupled simulator
details: Sim RL on 4k synthesized OpenClaw environments (seeded from a small pool of real Claw Agent traces, varied along environment-state and task axes, with generated rubric verifiers); policy = Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, up to 50 turns, evaluated Avg@3 on Claw-Eval and QwenClawBench; simulator ablation vs Qwen3.6-Plus.

Controllable simulation: (a) MCP environment adaptation with initial state + environment summary + control instructions injecting errors, pagination, withheld intermediate results; evaluated on Tool Decathlon and MCPMark. (b) 1k self-consistent fictional search worlds built from 300–500-row synthetic relational databases with SQL-derived ground truth and reverse-generated queries; evaluated on WideSearch (item/row F1) and compared against Real RL against a live search engine.

concrete_detailed_setting.aspect: Application II: world model as unified agent foundation
details: LWM RL (single-turn next-state prediction, no tool calls) applied as warm-up on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-SFT, then evaluated with no further fine-tuning on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Terminus-2, 5 runs), SWE-Bench Verified/Pro (internal scaffold, 3 rollouts), WideSearch, and OOD Claw-Eval, QwenClawBench, BFCL v4; 256k max sequence length.

Mechanistic analysis: identify turns whose thinking traces contain explicit environment-state predictions and score them against actual feedback; qualitative analysis of 129 thinking traces across four text domains.

key_findings.finding: Dedicated three-stage world-model training makes a mid-size open model competitive with, and the large model superior to, frontier LLMs at agentic environment simulation.
key_findings.evidence: On AgentWorldBench, Qwen-AgentWorld-397B-A17B scores 58.71 average versus GPT-5.4 58.25 and Claude Opus 4.6 57.80, leading on Terminal (57.73 vs 53.69) and SWE (68.49 vs 66.29); LWM training lifts the 35B base from 47.73 to 56.39 (+8.66) and the 397B base from 54.74 to 58.71, while untrained Qwen3.6 checkpoints reach only 50.81–52.42. GUI domains remain led by Claude Opus (≈61 vs 59.69), and Search is hardest for all models (best 37.82); Factuality is the weakest rubric dimension across all three candidate judges.

key_findings.finding: World-model RL on single-turn, tool-free next-state prediction transfers broadly to multi-turn tool-calling agent performance, including domains absent from world-model training.
key_findings.evidence: With no further fine-tuning, LWM RL warm-up on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-SFT improves Terminal-Bench 2.0 33.25→39.55, SWE-Bench Verified 64.47→67.86, SWE-Bench Pro 42.18→47.42, WideSearch item F1 33.38→46.17, and out-of-domain Claw-Eval +11.28, QwenClawBench +9.67, BFCL v4 62.29→71.25 (+8.96). Accuracy of explicit in-trace environment predictions on Terminal-Bench 2.0 trajectories rises from 69.9% to 78.3%, with a mailman case study where correct prediction of Postfix recipient validation ordering redirects the fix to local_recipient_maps.

key_findings.finding: Controllability, not raw simulation, is what makes simulator-based agent RL work — and it can beat training against the real environment.
key_findings.evidence: Uncontrolled Sim RL on MCP gives no gain (Tool Decathlon 32.4→31.5, MCPMark 21.5→24.6), whereas control instructions yield Tool Decathlon +3.7 and MCPMark +12.3. In Search, agents trained entirely in invented fictional worlds gain +16.29 item F1 / +10.49 row F1 at 35B and +3.87/+6.05 at 397B on real WideSearch, and controllable Sim RL reaches 50.3% item F1 vs 45.6% for Real RL against a live search engine; behaviorally, Sim RL raises web_extractor calls 2.5→4.0 per trajectory while Real RL drops them to 1.5, reflecting the deliberately snippet-withholding simulation design.

key_findings.finding: World-model RL reinforces domain-transferable environment knowledge rather than domain-specific output formats.
key_findings.evidence: Running Stage-3 RL on Terminal data alone improves Terminal by +14.2 (32.8→47.0) within 100 steps while all held-out text domains improve in parallel: SWE +11.5 (52.0→63.5), Search +11.8 (20.2→32.0), MCP +5.0 (53.5→58.5), with gains emerging in the first 10 steps and remaining stable.

key_findings.finding: Stable RL for language world modeling requires decomposed rubric rewards with a rule-based anchor and unique per-trajectory prediction targets.
key_findings.evidence: Expanding a trajectory into multiple turn-level RL samples with shared long prefixes collapses reward (an 'Echo Trap'), fixed by one turn per trajectory; a pairwise reference-reward converges slowly due to sparse, unstable judge preferences and a Turing-test reward barely converges due to high false negatives, while the five-dimensional rubric plus 10% rule verifier converges stably and mitigates self-praise reward hacking (further curbed by content-type classification and strict tag extraction). Simulator quality also matters downstream: Sim RL with Qwen3.6-Plus yields only +1.3/-0.1 on Claw-Eval/QwenClawBench versus +4.3/+7.1 with Qwen-AgentWorld-397B-A17B.
